items.label: text
items.text: Notice that water is always fed into the condenser at the lower end. That way it fills the condenser jacket better and if the flow of water stops for any reason the condenser jacket remains full of water.

items.label: text
items.text: The fractionating column is often packed with glass beads or something similar, although the separation of ethanol and water in the lab works perfectly well just with an empty column. For reasons that are beyond International GCSE, a high surface area in the column helps separation of the two vapours. The ethanol produced by this experiment is about 96% pure. For complicated reasons, again beyond International GCSE, it is impossible to remove the last 4% of water by distillation.

items.label: text
items.text: Simple distillation can be used to separate the components of a solution. Although we can use crystallisation to separate sodium chloride from a sodium chloride solution, we can also collect the water if we use simple distillation.

items.label: text
items.text: The water boils and is condensed back to a liquid by the condenser. The salt remains in the flask.

items.label: caption
items.text: Figure 2.9 Distilling pure water from sodium chloride solution.

items.label: text
items.text: You could, of course, collect the salt from the solution as well as collecting pure water. The sodium chloride solution eventually becomes so concentrated that the salt will crystallise out.

items.label: text
items.text: Fractionaldistillation is used to separate a mixture of liquids such as ethanol (alcohol) and water. Ethanol and water are completely miscible with each other. That means you can mix them together in any proportion and they will form a single liquid layer. You can separate them by taking advantage of their different boiling points: water boils at 100 °C, ethanol at 78 °C.
